metadata.title: On weight initialization in deep neural networks

nodes.name: Weight-initialization variance-matching problem
nodes.statement: The problem can be stated as follows: If the weights in a neural network are initialized using samples from a normal distribution, ${\cal{N}}(0,v^{2})$, how should  $v^{2}$ be chosen to ensure that the variance of the outputs from the different layers are approximately the same?
nodes.statement_short: How to choose the per-layer weight variance $v^2$ so activation variance is preserved across layers.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio \cite{glorot2010understanding} who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer. Although the paper makes several assumptions about the inputs to the model, it works extremely well in many cases and is widely used in the initialization of neural networks to date; this initialization scheme is commonly referred to as the  {\it{Xavier initialization}}.
differentia: the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer
nodes.statement_short: Glorot & Bengio's initialization $v^2=1/N$ for linear/near-linear activations.

nodes.name: He initialization
nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues \cite{he2015delving} argue that the {\it{Xavier initialization}} does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$ (commonly referred to as the {\it{He initialization}}). In support of their initialization, they provide an example of a 30 layer neural network which converges with the {\it{He initialization}}, but not under the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: He et al.'s RELU-targeted initialization $v^2=2/N$.

nodes.name: IID zero-mean Gaussian weight assumption
nodes.statement: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$.

nodes.name: IID first-layer input assumption
nodes.statement: Consistent with the assumptions in \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving}, I assume that the inputs to the first layer are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

nodes.name: Large-N (wide hidden layer) assumption
nodes.statement: I make the additional assumption that the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'; this assumption is reasonable given that most neural networks have several hundred nodes in the hidden layers.

nodes.name: Proposition 1 (weight/input independence)
nodes.statement: During the first iteration, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$
assumptions: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$.
I assume that the inputs to the first layer are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.
conclusions: $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$
nodes.statement_short: A layer's weights are independent of that layer's (and any other layer's) inputs.

nodes.name: Proposition 2 (asymptotic normality of pre-activations)
nodes.statement: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.
assumptions: I make the additional assumption that the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'
conclusions: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Each pre-activation is asymptotically Gaussian by the Central Limit Theorem.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$. Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$
nodes.statement_short: x_m(k) is a non-linear function of earlier, independent weights/inputs, so the m-th layer's weights stay independent of it (and of products of such terms).

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement:
For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right)  = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$,
\be 
\begin{split}
Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\
&=  E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\
&= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ 
\end{split}
\ee
where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}. This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that  $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus,  $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to  to be approximately normally distributed  during most iterations.
nodes.statement_short: The pre-activation is a sum of i.i.d. (or weakly-dependent) terms, so the CLT gives approximate normality for large N.

nodes.name: General weight-initialization formula for activations differentiable at 0
nodes.statement:
When $g(x)$ is differentiable at 0, we can perform a Taylor expansion in \eref{in2} about $E(y_{m}(i)) = 0$. Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored, 
\be 
x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205}
\ee 
Taking the expectation in \eref{in205} gives
\be 
\mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206}
\ee
This equation suggests that the expected value of the inputs to the $(m+1)^{th}$ layer has little dependence on the moments of the inputs to the ${m}^{th}$ layer. Using this result recursively suggests that for all layers (barring the first), 
\be 
\mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}.
\ee 
Using \eref{in204} and \eref{in2061}, the variance of $x_{m+1}(i)$ can be computed from \eref{in205} as 
\be 
\begin{split}
s_{m+1}^{2} = Var(x_{m+1}(i)) &\approx (g'(0))^{2} Var(y_{m}(i)) \\ 
&= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ 
&= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + g(0)^{2}) . \enum{in207}
\end{split}
\ee 
Using the condition $s_{m}^{2} \approx s_{m-1}^{2} ... = s_{1}^{2} = 1$ along with \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207} gives
\be 
v^{2} = \frac{1}{N(g'(0))^{2}(1+g(0)^{2})}, \enum{in208}
\ee
nodes.statement_short: A first-order Taylor expansion of the activation at 0 gives $v^2=1/(N g'(0)^2(1+g(0)^2))$ as the variance-preserving weight scale for any activation differentiable at 0.

nodes.name: Weight initialization for hyperbolic tangent activation (recovers Xavier)
nodes.statement:
For the hyperbolic tangent 
\be 
g(x) =\mbox{tanh}(x),
\ee
we have $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$. Plugging these results in \eref{in208} yields
\be 
v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{tanh1}
\ee 
which is precisely the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: Specializing to tanh ($g(0)=0,g'(0)=1$) recovers the Xavier scale $v\approx 1/\sqrt{N}$.

nodes.name: Weight initialization for sigmoid activation
nodes.statement:
For the sigmoid activation defined as
\be 
g(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \mbox{e}^{-x}}
\ee
we have $g(0) = 0.5$, $g'(0) = 1/4$. Plugging these values in \eref{in208} yields
\be 
v \approx \frac{3.6}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{relur}
\ee
nodes.statement_short: Specializing to the sigmoid ($g(0)=0.5,g'(0)=1/4$) gives $v\approx 3.6/\sqrt{N}$.

nodes.name: CIFAR-10 10-layer sigmoid convergence comparison
nodes.statement: First, I train the neural network with the {\it{Xavier initialization}} for 10 iterations and compute the top 5 accuracy on the validation dataset for each iteration. Next, I repeat the process using the initialization stated in \eref{relur}. A comparison of the validation accuracies for the 2 cases is provided in Figure \ref{fig:conv}, which shows that the convergence appears to stall with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, but proceeds rapidly with the initialization proposed in \eref{relur}.
nodes.statement_short: A 10-layer CIFAR-10 sigmoid network: Xavier stalls while the derived initialization converges quickly.

nodes.name: RELU weight-initialization formula (derivation of He initialization)
nodes.statement:
Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0, the results from \erefs{in205}{in207} cannot be used to compute the optimal value of $v^{2}$. To proceed, I use proposition 2 and \eref{in201} which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$. The mean will be given by
\be 
 \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1}
\ee 
Similarly,
\be 
E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) =  \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2}
\ee 
Using \eref{relu1} and \eref{relu2},
\be
s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3}
\ee 
For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2}  \approx 1$ which yields 
\be 
u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301}
\ee 
Plugging \eref{relu301} in \eref{relu1} yields $\mu_{m+1} \approx 0.7$. By the symmetry of the problem during the first iteration, we expect $\mu_{m+1} \approx \mu_{m} ... \approx \mu_{2} \approx 0.7$. 
Using this result in \eref{in204} yields
\be 
3 = Nv^{2}(1+ 0.49) 
\ee 
or 
\be 
v^{2}\approx 2/N,
\ee 
which is consistent with that obtained by \cite{he2015delving}.
assumptions: Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0
nodes.statement_short: Computing the truncated-Gaussian mean/variance of a RELU output and matching variance to 1 gives $v^2\approx 2/N$, a rigorous derivation of the He initialization.

nodes.name: Exponential decay of mean/variance under Xavier initialization with RELU
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
nodes.statement_short: Under Xavier-style $v^2=1/N$ with RELU, activation mean and variance decay geometrically like $(0.51)^{m-1}$, explaining why very deep RELU nets fail to converge under Xavier initialization.

nodes.name: Why deeper tanh layers have more unsaturated nodes
nodes.statement: In their analysis of a neural network with the hyperbolic tangent activations, \cite{glorot2010understanding}  find that the deeper layers in the neural network have a greater proportion of unsaturated nodes than the shallower layers. As is stated in their paper, `why this is happening remains to be understood'.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Why do deeper tanh layers end up less saturated than shallow ones?

nodes.name: Pre-activation recursion
nodes.statement: y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1}
nodes.statement_short: Defines the pre-activation $y_m(i)$ as a weighted sum of the previous layer's activations.

nodes.name: Activation recursion
nodes.statement: x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2}
nodes.statement_short: Defines the next layer's activation as the non-linearity applied to the pre-activation.

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance recursion
nodes.statement_short: Variance of the pre-activation in terms of the weight variance and the previous layer's second moment.

nodes.name: Variance recursion under Taylor-expansion approximation
nodes.statement_short: Variance recursion for differentiable activations via the Taylor-expansion approximation.

nodes.name: Sequential variance contraction with tanh under Glorot's uniform init
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Under Glorot's uniform initialization, tanh pre-activation variance shrinks by a factor of 3 at each layer.

nodes.name: PDF of a tanh-transformed Gaussian pre-activation
nodes.statement:
f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1},
\ee
where 
\be 
t_{y} =  \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right).
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form pdf of a tanh-transformed Gaussian pre-activation (Godfrey 2009).

nodes.name: Tanh-pdf vs. Glorot & Bengio simulation comparison
nodes.statement: Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$  (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding}  suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: The derived tanh-pdf plots reproduce the saturation trend Glorot & Bengio observed by simulation.

nodes.name: Saturation decreases with depth under tanh activation
nodes.statement: From the results in \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, we expect the  activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1. Accordingly, since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
assumptions: since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$
conclusions: we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network
nodes.statement_short: Decreasing pre-activation variance across depth predicts increasingly saturated tanh activations in shallower layers and less saturation in deeper layers.

nodes.name: Backward-pass variance constraint is unnecessary
nodes.statement: In their calculations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving} impose an additional set of constraints to ensure that the variance is maintained even during the backward pass. I believe that this is not required, since the requirement that the variance of the inputs at each layer be the same ensures that the gradient flows through in the backward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Argues the usual backward-pass variance constraint is unnecessary once forward-pass variance is matched at every layer.

nodes.name: Express x_m(k) via earlier weights/inputs
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer.
nodes.statement_short: x_m(k) is a non-linear function of weights/inputs from earlier layers.

nodes.name: Independence of m-th layer weights from that function
nodes.statement: Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities.
nodes.statement_short: Independence propagates through any non-linear function of independent quantities.

nodes.name: Conclude W_m(i,j) independent of x_m(k)
nodes.statement: Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: States the independence conclusion for the proposition.

nodes.name: Extend to independence of products
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$
nodes.statement_short: Extends the independence result to products of inputs, used later.

nodes.name: Mean of p_ij is 0
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right)  = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Computes $E(p_{ij})=0$.

nodes.name: Covariance of p_ij, p_ik is 0
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, for $j \neq k$,
\be 
\begin{split}
Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\
&=  E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\
&= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ 
\end{split}
\ee
where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}.
nodes.statement_short: Shows $p_{ij}$ and $p_{ik}$ are uncorrelated, invoking the earlier independence identity.

nodes.name: p_ij are iid
nodes.statement: This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables.
nodes.statement_short: Concludes the $p_{ij}$ terms are i.i.d.

nodes.name: Apply the Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
nodes.statement_short: Invokes the CLT to get approximate normality for large N.

nodes.name: Relaxation to weakly dependent, non-identical terms
nodes.statement: Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that  $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}).
nodes.statement_short: Notes the CLT conclusion still holds under weaker dependence conditions.

nodes.name: Conclude approximate normality
nodes.statement: Thus,  $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to  to be approximately normally distributed  during most iterations.
nodes.statement_short: States the proposition's conclusion.
